state.title: Demonstrate single-threaded event loop ordering

parts.text:
The waiting happens at the OS/driver level, not on a JS thread. When you call the DB driver, it hands the actual socket read off to the operating system and immediately returns control to Node. Node's single JS thread keeps running other code (other requests, timers, etc). When the OS says "the DB responded," Node puts your `.then`/resumed-function work on the event loop's queue, and the single JS thread picks it up once it's free.

That's why "start" and "end" print before "promise done" above — the synchronous code always finishes first, and queued async work runs after, but it's all still one thread taking turns, not two threads running at once.

parts.text: Whose branch it is doesn't determine whether force-push is safe — whether anyone *else* has it checked out or has pushed to it does. Rebasing rewrites commit hashes, so after a rebase your local history and the remote's history diverge; `git push --force` overwrites whatever is on the remote with your rewritten history, unconditionally. If a teammate had pulled that branch, or pushed a small commit to it while you were rebasing, force-push throws that away with no warning. Is anyone else working off `feat/topic-filters`?

parts.text: Nothing local recovers sam's pushed commits since your local reflog only has *your* history, not what was briefly on the remote before you overwrote it — but this is recoverable: sam almost certainly still has his commits in his own local reflog or working copy, since he committed and pushed them himself. Have him check `git reflog` locally and re-push, or just cherry-pick from his local branch onto yours. Going forward, use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `--force` — it refuses to push if the remote has commits you haven't seen locally, which would have caught this before it happened.
ok pinged him, he still has it locally so we're fine. i guess i just assumed force-pushing was harmless as long as *i* was the one running the command

That's the core misconception worth remembering: force-push safety depends on whether the branch is shared, not on who's typing the command. On a shared branch, always assume someone else might have unpushed or unpulled work, use `--force-with-lease` by default, and give teammates a heads up before rewriting history on a branch they're also using.
